Improving vendor management, sales and customer experience

A case study from my work as Business Development Manager at Socheko.com, 2018–2021.

The context

A business with potential, and a process that needed structure

While working in business development at Socheko.com, I found problems in four areas: vendor management, sales processes, payment arrangements and product organisation.

Vendor agreements

Existing vendor agreements were inconsistent in structure and management.

Read more

Agreements with existing vendors varied in margins, terms and conditions, and delivery arrangements. Contracts weren’t reviewed regularly, which made vendor relationships and expectations harder to manage.

Payment and commercial terms

Margins, payment terms and commercial procedures needed clearer definition.

Read more

Margin ratios, payment terms and operational procedures needed to be documented and standardised. Without consistent commercial guidelines, misunderstandings and disagreements with vendors were increasing.

Product categorisation

Vendors and their products needed a more systematic category structure.

Read more

We needed a consistent category structure to organise products and assign vendors by what they supplied, and a dedicated category manager was appointed for this work. Vendors also had to provide accurate product information, descriptions and high-quality photos in the website’s required format, so listings stayed consistent.

Customer needs

Customer feedback needed to feed into product and business decisions.

Read more

Customer Service conversations revealed preferences, recurring issues and unmet needs. That information had to reach the right teams to guide product selection, priorities and business improvements.

The approach

From business problem to structured process

      Business requirements I shared with the IT team

      Sales visibility

      Sales and order activity, to support vendor performance monitoring.

      Product information

      Structured product details, descriptions, photos and updates.

      Hot-selling products

      Visibility of popular products, to support product selection.

      Comments and communication

      A way for vendors to share comments, updates and information with us.

      The outcomes

      What changed

      Better vendor coordination, clearer commercial processes, organised products and real use of customer feedback gave us a more structured way to manage vendors and make business decisions.

      More structured vendor management

      Vendor relationships, agreements and product categories became systematically organised, so responsibilities and information were easier to manage.

      Fewer payment issues

      Clearer payment terms, margin ratios and agreements reduced misunderstandings and payment problems with vendors.

      Better customer understanding

      Customer feedback gave useful insight into expectations, product preferences and areas to improve.

      Support for sales and satisfaction

      Better-organised vendors, more complete product information and attention to customer needs supported product selection, sales and customer satisfaction.

      Commercial processesUnclear margins, payment terms and responsibilitiesClear commercial agreements and expectations

Behind it sat months of planning: booking the venue, filling 50+ stalls, bringing in sponsors and media partners, and making sure a crowd of 200+ guests had a great, safe day.

      Organic soapberries

      A farm-to-market business plan I led during my product sourcing and development work at Bleschu.dk: from remote villages in Far-West Nepal to buyers abroad.

      My roleBusiness Counselor, Product Sourcing & Development
      SourcingDarchula, Far-West Nepal
      ProductsShells · Seeds · Powder
      Bleschu’s aimMake everyday cleaning sustainable

      A green business with a fair-trade idea

      Soapberries are a natural cleaning product grown in Nepal’s hills. Production had been falling and farmers were getting little in return, so I built a business plan to source directly from the villages, process and pack the berries in Kathmandu, and sell them under our own brand.

      • Green, organic product with fair returns to farmers, society, customers and the environment
      • Expand and diversify the organic range over time
      • Build a trusted brand through steady, sustainable growth
      Soapberry shellsThe main product, sold in 250 g, 500 g and 1 kg packs
      Soapberry seedsA by-product with its own buyers
      Soapberry powderReady-to-use form for detergent and cosmetics
      70%India

      Where Nepal’s soapberries go

      Estimated share of the market, from my research. Hover a row to highlight it.

      • India70%
      • Nepal20%
      • Europe5%
      • China and others5%

      The opportunity: exports through India were falling as new firms began shipping directly from Nepal to Australia, New Zealand and Europe. Selling direct, under our own brand, was the gap.

      SWOT analysis

      Strengths
      • Almost no competition
      • First-mover advantage
      • Knowledge of interested buyers and untouched production areas
      Weaknesses
      • Small team
      • Quality control
      • Limited technology
      • Reliance on outsourcing
      Opportunities
      • Rising demand in international markets
      • Low awareness in Nepal, so room to grow the home market
      • Diversifying into new products
      Threats
      • New competitors attracted by global demand
      • Delays while waiting for certification

      From village to customer in four steps

      1. 1ProcurementCollected by local farmers, transported to Kathmandu
      2. 2ProcessingDrying, cleaning and screening
      3. 3PackingKraft paper, cotton bags, cartons and jute sacks
      4. 4SupplyWarehousing or direct supply to customers

      My cost model per pack in US dollars. Estimates could move 10–15% with exchange rates. Pick a pack size:
